entities.summary:
André d'Espinay was a French Roman Catholic bishop and cardinal who played a crucial role in the Council of Trent (1545-1563), a pivotal event in the Counter-Reformation.

Born in 1470, d'Espinay was ordained as a priest in 1495 and rose through the ranks to become the Bishop of Bayeux in 1514. He was appointed as a cardinal in 1517 and served as the Camerlengo of the College of Cardinals from 1534 to 1547.

D'Espinay's significant contributions to the Council of Trent included his advocacy for Catholic orthodoxy and his efforts to reform the Catholic Church's governance and liturgy. His influence helped shape the Council's decrees, which had a profound impact on Catholic theology and practice.

The legacy of André d'Espinay can be seen in the continued influence of the Catholic Church in Western Europe during the 16th and 17th centuries. His contributions to the Council of Trent also paved the way for the development of Catholic theology and liturgy in the modern era.

One striking statistic about d'Espinay's life is that he was one of the few cardinals who did not attend the infamous Sack of Rome in 1527, a brutal attack on the city by the Holy Roman Empire's troops.

"We must not be afraid of reform, for it is through reform that we find true obedience to God," d'Espinay once said in a statement to the Council of Trent.

His involvement in the Church's governance and doctrine helped to establish a framework that would shape the institution for centuries to come.


In conclusion, André d'Espinay was an important figure in the history of the Catholic Church, whose contributions had significant regional implications for the development of Western European Christianity.
